expectations.text: Output warns that a single Louvain run reflects modularity DEGENERACY — many qualitatively different partitions have near-equal modularity (Good et al.) — not just random stochasticity
expectations.evidence: The response frames the problem purely as non-determinism/seed variation: 'Louvain is non-deterministic. If you run it once and report Q = 0.67, a reviewer will ask whether this is the lucky run.' It never uses the words 'degenerate' or 'degeneracy,' and never mentions that the modularity landscape contains exponentially many near-optimal partitions that are qualitatively different (Good et al.). The concern is cast as 'does Q vary across runs?' not as a fundamental degeneracy of the objective function.

expectations.text: Output frames stability analysis as a PREREQUISITE before naming or interpreting communities, not as an optional improvement step
expectations.evidence: Section 2 ('Name Communities by Intellectual Content, Not by Topology') presents a full four-step naming workflow before any stability check is introduced. Stability appears in Section 3 as a reporting template and in Section 6 as a caveat under 'Multiple runs.' The structure is: name first, check stability later. Stability is never framed as a gate that must be passed before naming is meaningful.

expectations.text: Output recommends running community detection many times (e.g., 100+ runs) and measuring pairwise stability with ARI, NMI, or similar
expectations.evidence: Section 3 explicitly recommends 'run the algorithm 100 times with different random seeds and computed the normalized mutual information (NMI) between each pair of partitions.' Section 6 adds 'run the algorithm at least 50–100 times.' NMI is named as the stability metric and Lancichinetti & Fortunato (2012) on consensus clustering is cited.

expectations.text: Output recommends comparing Q = 0.67 against a configuration-model null (random graphs with the same degree sequence) rather than accepting it at face value
expectations.evidence: The response opens by accepting Q = 0.67 as 'genuinely high' and 'strong' ('anything above 0.3 is conventionally considered meaningful; above 0.6 is strong'). No null model comparison is recommended anywhere in the response. The configuration model, random graph baseline, or degree-sequence-preserving null are never mentioned.

expectations.text: Output mentions Louvain resolution limit or the alternative of SBM (Stochastic Block Model) for more principled partitioning
expectations.evidence: Section 6 explicitly addresses the 'Resolution limit': 'Louvain with γ = 1.0 may merge small but cohesive clusters and may miss structure within large communities. If any community has more than ~400 nodes, consider whether it warrants recursive partitioning.' SBM is not mentioned, but the resolution limit is covered clearly.
